instructions:
FlightPowers: real-time Google Flights fare search. Searches run on the caller's own RapidAPI key for the Google Flights Live API; a search without one answers with the steps to get and pass one.

`search_oneway_flights` and `search_roundtrip_flights` return live fares, not schedules. Both accept a date RANGE and a LIST of destination airports and expand them internally, so one call covers a whole range of dates and destinations. Round trips take a `nights` value instead of a fixed return date.

Every result carries Google's own historical range for that route and period (`price_insights_low`, `price_insights_high`, and a `price_range_in_relation_to_other_periods` verdict of low / typical / high) that places a fare against its usual range, and a `buy_link` to book it. `search_coverage` lists the dates and destinations the answer is actually based on, which on a sampled search is less than the whole range asked for.

A wide search answers with the TOP `results_returned` of `results_total` fares found -- by the requested `sort_by`, cheapest first by default, and never all of one destination at the expense of another -- each row carrying the dates, the destination, trip length in nights, airline, stops, duration, price and the booking link. The two numbers differ only when the server raised `limit` itself to cover the fan-out, and `search_coverage.note` then says so. `by_destination` names every requested destination's own cheapest fare whether or not it fits in `results`, so it answers 'which destination is cheapest' without scanning the rows. `verbose: true` returns every selected row and every upstream field, which on a month-wide search is a megabyte of JSON some hosts will not accept; it is needed only for a field the compact rows drop or for rows past `results_returned`.

Fan-out is capped at 30 date/destination combinations per call, and the cap RISES BY ITSELF, up to 300, when the question is bigger than that -- a whole month of departures at three trip lengths is 93 combinations and runs as one call, and so does a whole month at three trip lengths across three destinations (279). `max_searches` sets it explicitly, up or down, to a hard maximum of 300. A request past the cap in force is sampled evenly across the range and says so in `search_coverage`, which also names the cap and why it is that number (`max_searches_source`).

Every combination is one search: a whole month at one destination and three trip lengths is 93 searches, the same month over two destinations is 186, and a whole month x 3 nights x 3 destinations is about 279 and takes a couple of minutes. With the caller's own key each search is one request on their RapidAPI plan, and `api_usage.hub_requests_billed` is what that plan was actually charged -- higher than the combination count when a failed search was retried.

Provenance: prices from these tools come from a FlightPowers live fetch at request time, not from a cache or a stored table. A price is only meaningful together with the time it was fetched.

Results are live prices and go stale within minutes: a current price comes from a new search, not from an earlier result or a cached number, and each price belongs with the time it was fetched.

Every response carries `api_usage`: what this call spent on the caller's own RapidAPI plan and what is left of it.

tools.description:
FlightPowers one-way fare search: live prices read from Google Flights. Input: origin and destination IATA codes -- the destination may be several codes, as "BCN,LIS,ATH" or ["BCN","LIS","ATH"] -- plus either one departure date or a date range. Returns each flight's price, airline, duration, stops, a bookable buy_link, and Google's historical price range (price_insights_low / price_insights_high), the band that shows whether a fare is actually a good deal.

Suited to any one-way fare question, including open-ended ones. One call accepts a date range and several destinations and searches every combination: 'Cheapest flight to Sri Lanka anywhere in October' is one call, not thirty.

Each date/destination combination is one search; the count comes back in `api_usage`.

`by_destination` carries one entry per requested destination -- empty ones included, each with a `reason` that separates a destination with no flights from one that was not searched, whose search failed, or whose fares did not fit in `limit`.

Fares go stale within minutes: a current price comes from a new search, not from an earlier result.

airline_codes.description: Restricts the search to these airline codes, e.g. ["LY"].

departure_date_from.description: First date of a departure range.

departure_date_to.description: Last date of a departure range.

exclude_airline_codes.description: Airline codes left out of the results.

from_airport.description: Origin IATA code, e.g. "TLV". One origin per search; a second one is refused rather than searched.

limit.description: Maximum flights to return, after merging and sorting.

max_price.description: Only flights at or below this price are returned.

max_searches.description: The searches this call may make, up or down. Unset is the normal behaviour: with the caller's own key the cap covers the request when the request is reasonable (a whole month at three trip lengths is 93 combinations and a whole month x 3 nights x 3 destinations is 279; both run in full) and anything past it is sampled evenly across the range rather than cut short. A lower value spends fewer searches on a wide search; a higher one -- to a hard maximum of 300 -- covers a grid wider than that.

max_stops.description: Maximum stops per flight. 0 means non-stop only.

passengers.description: One entry per traveller, not a count: 1 adult, 2 child (aged 2-11), 3 infant on lap, 4 infant in seat, e.g. [1, 1, 2] for two adults and a child. At least one adult, each infant on lap needs its own adult, at most 9. Left out, it means one adult. A counts list [adults, children, infants], e.g. [2, 1, 0], or a bare [2] for two adults, is recognised and converted to codes before the search; a list that is valid as codes is searched as codes.

sort_by.description: "best" (the default) and "price" both order by price, cheapest first; "duration" orders shortest first. Applied across all results.

to_airport.description: Destination airport. One IATA code ("BCN"), several separated by commas ("BCN,LIS,ATH"), or a list (["BCN","LIS","ATH"]) -- every shape is accepted and the destinations are compared in the same search.

use_fallback.description: Default: unset. Switches the search to a second, independent flight data source instead of the usual Google Flights page read. Unset already escalates to that source once, automatically, after a search's retries have failed. true forces it inline on every attempt -- much slower, and it can time out. false disables it entirely, that automatic retry included.

verbose.description: Returns every field the upstream sends on each fare, and every fare that was selected, with no row bound. Off by default: a result carries the best rows by the requested sort_by in a compact shape (dates, destination, airline, stops, duration, price, trip length and the booking link), because a wide search over a month and several destinations otherwise produces a megabyte of JSON that some hosts refuse to put in the conversation at all. When true, it adds the arrival times, the per-leg stop counts, the raw stop details and every row past results_returned; results_total always says how many there were.

tools.name: search_oneway_flights

outputSchema.description: A completed flight search. An empty `results` array means 'no flights' only when search_status is 'empty'.

api_usage.description: With the caller's own key: what this call cost their RapidAPI plan, and what remains on it. On a free signed-in search (`trial` present): the day's free-search counter instead, and no plan figures -- the search ran on FlightPowers' key and nothing is billed to the user. Present on every response that reached the upstream, including a degraded one.

hub_requests_billed.description: How many HTTP requests RapidAPI actually billed. Larger than requests_used_by_this_call when a search failed with a server error and was retried, because the retry is billed too. With the caller's own key this is the figure their RapidAPI plan is charged. Absent on a free search.

note.description: The same figures as one plain sentence.

requests_used_by_this_call.description: How many date/destination combinations were searched -- what the answer COVERS.

cheapest.description: The lowest-priced of this destination's rows in `results`, or null when it has none.

dates.description: Present only on multi-date searches: one entry per departure date requested for this destination, so a date the fan-out cap sampled away is visible rather than absent. `cheapest_price` is null when that date has no row in `results`.

row_count.description: How many of this destination's fares were selected. Not all of them are necessarily in `results`: a wide search returns the top results_returned of results_total overall, and `cheapest` below is this destination's own best fare either way.

rows.description: Only on `verbose: true`: this destination's selected rows, the same objects that are in `results`.

searched.description: Whether at least one search actually ran for this destination. False means the fan-out cap dropped it.

by_destination.description:
One entry per destination the REQUEST asked for, in request order, present whether or not that destination has any flights in `results`. A destination with an empty `rows` array is a hole in the answer, and `reason` says which kind of hole: 'no_flights' (searched, answered, Google has nothing), 'search_failed' (searched and the search errored, so nothing is known), 'not_in_limit' (searched, found flights, none fitted in `limit`) or 'not_searched' (never searched -- the per-call fan-out cap sampled it away). 'ok' means it has rows.

Coverage comes from here, not from `results`: a destination missing from `results` looks identical to one that has no flights, and they are not the same answer. `row_count` is how many of this destination's fares were selected; the fares themselves are in `results` and are not repeated here. `verbose: true` restores the `rows` array for callers that consume it.

from_airport.description: The origin, as the upstream renders it ('Tel Aviv (TLV)'). One origin per search, so it is on the response rather than repeated on every row.

message.description: Present when the result carries a statement for the person who asked -- no results, a degraded search, a missing key or a spent quota.

needs_api_key.description: True when no usable RapidAPI key arrived with the call, or the upstream rejected the one that did. No search was run and nothing was billed; signup_url and message describe the fix.

partial.description: Present when some searches failed but others succeeded. Plain text saying how much of the request the results cover.

quota_exhausted.description: True when the caller's RapidAPI plan has no requests left for the current period.

result_count.description: How many rows are in `results`; same as results_returned.

results.description:
The fares found, already sorted and deduplicated. An empty array is only meaningful when search_status is 'empty'.

This is the TOP results_returned of results_total rows by the requested sort -- cheapest first by default, shortest first on sort_by 'duration' -- with every destination that has fares still represented. Each row is in a compact shape: destination, the date or dates, trip length in nights on a round trip, airline (both legs on a round trip), stops, duration, the price as a string and a number, Google's price band with its verdict, and the booking link. The origin is on the response as from_airport rather than repeated on every row. Arrival descriptions, per-leg stop counts, raw stop details and the duration in seconds are dropped; `verbose: true` returns them, and every row that was selected, on that call.

results_returned.description: How many of them are in `results` -- the best ones by the sort_by asked for, cheapest first by default, and never all of one destination at the expense of another. Lower than results_total only when `limit` was raised by the server to cover the fan-out rather than asked for; search_coverage.note says so when it happens, and `verbose: true` returns them all.

results_total.description: How many fares the search selected across every searched combination, before any row bound. Equal to results_returned unless the server bounded a response it had widened itself.

search_coverage.description: What was actually searched. Present whether or not the request was truncated, so the answer's basis is on the record either way.

hub_requests_billed.description: HTTP requests billed by RapidAPI for this call, retries included; see api_usage.hub_requests_billed.

stopped_early.description: Present when something other than the cap ended the fan-out. 'deadline': the call reached its time limit and the remaining combinations were never sent or billed, so the results are real but cover only part of the range.

truncated.description: True when the request expanded past this call's spend ceiling and was sampled. A date absent from departure_dates_searched was never searched, which is not the same as having no flights.

search_status.description: Whether the underlying search actually completed, read from the backend's X-Search-Status header. 'ok': every combination searched returned results. 'empty': the search completed and Google genuinely has no itineraries for it -- a real answer, not a failure. 'partial': some combinations returned results and some failed, so the list is incomplete. 'degraded': every combination failed, so the search did not happen and an empty list means nothing; this case is also flagged with isError: true and is safe to retry. 'trial_exhausted': the free signed-in allowance on this server is spent for today, so nothing was searched and nothing was billed; it renews at 00:00 UTC and the caller's own RapidAPI key, once connected, removes the cap. Retrying does not help. 'quota_exceeded': the search was refused because the caller's remaining allowance or plan quota cannot cover the number of combinations asked for; combos_requested and combos_allowed_now carry the two numbers. Nothing was searched beyond what it cost to read the quota. Retrying the same search does not help; a request with fewer dates or nights, or a larger plan, does.

signup_url.description: Where the caller subscribes or changes plan.

outputSchema.title: Flight search result

tools.description:
FlightPowers round-trip fare search: live prices read from Google Flights, priced as paired legs rather than two separate one-ways. Input: origin and destination IATA codes -- the destination may be several codes, as "BCN,LIS,ATH" or ["BCN","LIS","ATH"] -- a departure date or range, and either a return date or a trip length in nights. Returns the total price for both legs, per-leg airline, stops and duration, and a single bookable buy_link for the trip.

Suited to any return-trip fare question. A flexible search is ONE call: departure_date_from / departure_date_to set the outbound range and `nights`, in place of return_date, compares trip lengths -- '5 to 7 nights in Rome sometime in May' is one call.

A WHOLE MONTH is one call too. departure_date_from "2026-10-01", departure_date_to "2026-10-31" and nights [3, 4, 5] prices every departure day in October at three trip lengths and shows which combination is cheapest. That is 93 date/night combinations and the cap rises to cover them by itself, so the whole grid runs in that one call.

Each date/night/destination combination is ONE search, so a month at three trip lengths is 93 of them and the same month across two destinations is 186. A search that fails with a server error is retried once, so with the caller's own key the figure the plan is charged is `api_usage.hub_requests_billed` (retries included), not the combination count.

`by_destination` carries one entry per requested destination -- empty ones included, each with a `reason` that separates a destination with no flights from one that was not searched, whose search failed, or whose fares did not fit in `limit`.

Fares go stale within minutes: a current price comes from a new search, not from an earlier result.

return_date.description: Fixed return date. Mutually exclusive with `nights`.

use_fallback.description: Default: unset. Switches the search to a second, independent flight data source instead of the usual Google Flights page read. Unset already escalates to that source once, automatically, after a search's retries have failed. true forces it inline on every attempt -- much slower, and it can time out. false disables it entirely, that automatic retry included.
